Regardless of what it’s called, we’re clearly moving to yet another era of AI agents in our work. 

We’ve quickly jumped from agents that spit out a quick answer for you, to today agents that you orchestrate inside of a set of tasks. But as agents can both fan out and work in parallel, handle much larger context, be able to do long running work, and have far greater levels of capabilities, we’re entering yet another level of what we can have AI do for us.

We’ll soon be able to give agents a set of goals, and they can go out and design the best solution for that goal, while also continuously improving it based on the ongoing execution of whatever it built. This will obviously start with engineering because that’s where we’re seeing the best practices emerge first in almost every new era of agents. 

But the impact can be quite massive across the rest of knowledge work. You’ll tell an agent to improve your client onboarding workflow to achieve a certain targeted goal; or have agents go reduce risk in your business; or improve your security posture on an ongoing basis.

These autonomous systems will be able to take on a set of goals, design the best outcome, test and iterate, deploy, and then optimize whatever it built on an ongoing basis. Importantly, this leads to outcomes and results that humans literally couldn’t have accomplished before. This will lead to fairly new levels of productivity with AI.

ok after a full day of using gpt 6.2 astra and sol on my real projects, here's my review

tl;dr - they are not a drop-in replacement for fable 5.2 and opus 5.5, but they are _really good_ once you figured out how to use their strength

1. first, the quirks

i started called these the "gpt smell", which is still here with the 6.2 series

the models' judgment on when to ask the user about something and when to go ahead is just not quite right. it'll escalate trivial decisions where clearly only one option is preferable, or choose to go down a path by itself that makes significant tradeoffs that should have needed my eyes

so as a primary driver for "let me just talk to it about everything" type of use case, they aren't great - i'd say they are close to opus 5 in this regard, and far behind opus 5.5

2. but... i found something _really_ cool

having ultrafast on sol is completely insane. with astra, it burns my wallet ultrafast, but with sol it's actually quite affordable! 

the best use of sol on ultrafast that i've found is adversarial code reviews - they typically don't need to run a lot of heavy tool calls that would slow them down. most of the time is spent on the model, which gets massively accelerated by ultrafast

once you got a feel from using sol ultrafast as the code reviewer, you can never go back. it feels like pure magic

3. and... i found something else that's really cool

we are not supposed to ask the gpt 6.2 series to respond in text. we should let them respond in html! (i use lavish-axi, but you can just ask for html or use whatever fits in your harness)

i suspect they are post-trained specifically on their latest "intelligent UI" concept in chatgpt - these models are so good at visual presentations of ideas

once you allow the model to respond in visual artifacts, it's a completely different game. the reports and decisions explained by astra in html is a clear step function better than what fable and opus give me

so after a day of use, i've made two changes to my setup:
- always sol ultrafast as code reviewer
- i started preferring asking astra for planning in html artifacts over fable/opus. i think i'll keep a/b testing for a while to decide how much and for which case i fully switch over

all in all, i strongly recommend spending more time with these two models. don't expect them to be the "everything" model, but rather figure out where they fit best in your workflow. i couldn't be happier for the two use cases i found above, and i'm pretty sure there are more

GPT 6.2 Astra and GPT 6.2 Sol launched today. We've been running them through the Surge benchmark suite: 

11 benchmarks built by professional doctors, accountants, lawyers, and staff software engineers to test whether models can get through an ordinary Tuesday at work.

⚖️ DAYJOB: LAW, our new benchmark measuring whether agents can handle the work of experienced lawyers ⚖️

An investor is about to put $20 million into a startup. The company’s ownership spreadsheet looks clean. But its official stock ledger shows 350,000 shares held by a former executive that the spreadsheet leaves out. The board approved a buyback, but there’s no proof it ever happened.

Would an AI agent notice? Better question: would it do anything about it?

That’s one of the scenarios in DAYJOB: Law, our new benchmark for evaluating AI agents on real-world legal work, with 2,638 messy case files and nearly 1 GB of data to sort through.

The agent has to recognize that the missing shares could change the investor’s ownership stake and the price they should pay, even though the request never mentioned them.
